title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
pub: Science, vol. 384, no. 6702, pp. 1306–1308 (21 June 2024), doi 10.1126/science.adj0998, as 'GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs'; working-paper version arXiv:2303.10130 (March 2023, v5 August 2023)

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-level, selective-deployment framing and materially extends it by quantifying potential task exposure while distinguishing technical feasibility from realised productivity or automation. It also identifies complementary tooling, human-in-the-loop workflows and process reconfiguration as conditions for useful deployment.
qs: This exposure measure reflects an estimate of the technical capacity to make human labor more efficient; however, social, economic, regulatory, and other determinants imply that technical feasibility does not guarantee labor productivity or automation outcomes.
Developing these tools and integrating them into systems will require time and possibly significant reconfiguration of existing processes across various industries.

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between technical exposure and realised aggregate outcomes: its measurements concern LLM impact potential, while its claims about growing economic effects depend on future diffusion and complementary technologies rather than demonstrated productivity gains. It does not directly assess verification costs or employment reallocation.
qs: This paper’s primary contributions are to provide a set of measurements of LLM impact potential and to demonstrate the use case of applying LLMs to develop such measurements efficiently and at scale.
We also find that the potential impact of LLMs expands significantly when we take into account the development of complementary technologies.

kp.k: Exposure measures potential efficiency, not predicted job losses
kp.d: The supplied text is the August 2023 v5 working paper, although the document header also identifies the June 2024 Science publication. It defines task exposure as the potential to reduce completion time by at least 50% while maintaining equivalent quality. Exposure does not distinguish augmentation from displacement, and the authors explicitly decline to predict development or adoption timelines. Its estimates therefore concern technical potential rather than observed employment changes.
qs: We define exposure as a proxy for potential economic impact without distinguishing between labor-augmenting or labor-displacing effects.
Equivalent quality means that a third party, typically the recipient of the output, would not notice or care about LLM assistance.
We do not make predictions about the development or adoption timeline of such LLMs.

kp.k: Human and GPT-4 classifications underpin the exposure estimates
kp.d: The study uses O*NET 27.2, covering 1,016 occupations, 19,265 tasks and 2,087 Detailed Work Activities, alongside BLS employment and wage data from 2020 and 2021. Authors and annotators experienced with OpenAI models supplied human labels; an early GPT-4 classified task–occupation pairs using a prompt adjusted for agreement with author labels. The analysis distinguishes direct exposure (α), direct exposure plus half-weighted complementary-software exposure (β), and full combined exposure (ζ). Most analyses use β; some weight core tasks twice as heavily as supplemental tasks, while others use equal task weights.
qs: We use the O*NET 27.2 database (O*NET, 2023), which contains information on 1,016 occupations, including their respective Detailed Work Activities (DWAs) and tasks.
We obtain employment and wage data from the 2020 and 2021 Occupational Employment series provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In this analysis, we present results from human annotators as our primary results.

kp.k: Estimated exposure reaches much of the US workforce
kp.d: Using β, the authors estimate that 80% of workers belong to occupations with at least 10% task exposure and 19% belong to occupations with over half their tasks exposed. These are occupation-based estimates weighted to workers, not findings that those workers have lost employment. The abstract reports approximately 15% of tasks could be completed significantly faster using an LLM alone, increasing to 47–56% with complementary software and tooling.
qs: Based on the 𝛽 values, we estimate that 80% of workers belong to an occupation with at least 10% of its tasks exposed to LLMs, while 19% of workers are in an occupation where over half of its tasks are labeled as exposed.
Our analysis suggests that, with access to an LLM, about 15% of all worker tasks in the US could be completed significantly faster at the same level of quality.
When incorporating software and tooling built on top of LLMs, this share increases to between 47 and 56% of all tasks.

kp.k: Complementary software substantially expands potential task coverage
kp.d: The distinction between standalone models and integrated systems drives the results. Human assessments put only 3% of workers above half-task exposure with existing language and code capabilities alone, rising to as much as 49% when other generative models and complementary technologies are included. These scenarios differ from the preferred β estimate of 19%. The authors argue that realizing this broader potential requires investment, integration and potentially substantial process reconfiguration.
qs: Human assessments suggest that only 3% of U.S. workers have over half of their tasks exposed to LLMs when considering existing language and code capabilities without additional software or modalities.
Accounting for other generative models and complementary technologies, our human estimates indicate that up to 49% of workers could have half or more of their tasks exposed to LLMs.
Developing these tools and integrating them into systems will require time and possibly significant reconfiguration of existing processes across various industries.

kp.k: Legal research illustrates domain-specific integration and reliability mitigation
kp.d: The authors present Casetext as an example of specialized legal-research software using embeddings and summarization to counter inaccurate case or document details. They also include hypothetical software aggregating prior cases and drafting tailored legal research memoranda in their exposure rubric. These examples illustrate a proposed mechanism for improving legal workflows, rather than supplying a controlled evaluation of legal research accuracy or productivity.
qs: For example, Casetext offers LLM-based legal research tools that provide lawyers with quicker and more accurate legal research results, utilizing embeddings and summarization to counter the risk that GPT-4 could provide inaccurate details about a legal case or set of documents.
Software built for legal purposes that can quickly aggregate and summarize all previous cases in a particular legal area and write legal research memos tailored to the law firm’s needs

kp.k: Verification and trust constrain legal adoption
kp.d: The discussion identifies legal professionals’ need to check original documents or conduct independent research as a determinant of model usefulness. More generally, adoption depends on confidence, changed working habits, cost, flexibility, preferences, incentives, data availability and regulation. This is an adoption bottleneck argument, not a recommendation to dispense with verification or evidence that lawyers can safely rely on unchecked outputs.
qs: For instance, in the legal profession, the models’ usefulness depends on whether legal professionals can trust model outputs without verifying original documents or conducting independent research.
The cost and flexibility of the technology, worker and firm preferences, and incentives also significantly influence the adoption of tools built on top of LLMs.
Moreover, the adoption of LLMs will vary across different economic sectors due to factors such as data availability, regulatory environment, and the distribution of power and interests.

kp.k: Full task exposure does not establish full occupational automation
kp.d: Table 4 places Legal Secretaries and Administrative Assistants at 100.0% exposure under the model’s upper-bound ζ measure; Court Reporters and Simultaneous Captioners score 92.9% under model α and 96.4% under model β. These are classifications of potential time savings, not observed displacement. Humans classify 15 occupations as fully exposed under ζ, compared with 86 for GPT-4, illustrating differences between annotation sources.
qs: Humans labeled 15 occupations as "fully exposed."
The model labeled 86 occupations as "fully exposed."

As such, occupations listed in this table are those where we estimate that GPTs and GPT-powered software are able to save workers a significant amount of time completing a large share of their tasks, but it does not necessarily suggest that their tasks can be fully automated by these technologies.

kp.k: Higher wages and writing correlate with greater exposure
kp.d: Both annotation sources associate higher occupational wages with greater exposure, while also finding highly exposed lower-wage occupations. Regression results associate writing and programming with higher exposure and science and critical thinking with lower exposure. Exposure rises from Job Zone 1 to Job Zone 4, then remains similar or falls in Job Zone 5. Lawyers appear among Job Zone 5 examples; these group-level findings do not establish a lawyer-specific exposure rate or differences between junior lawyers and partners.
qs: While there are numerous low-wage occupations with high exposure and high-wage occupations with low exposure, the overall trend in the binscatter plot reveals that higher wages are associated with increased exposure to LLMs.

Our findings indicate that the importance of science and critical thinking skills are strongly negatively associated with exposure, suggesting that occupations requiring these skills are less likely to be impacted by current LLMs.

Conversely, programming and writing skills show a strong positive association with exposure, implying that occupations involving these skills are more susceptible to being influenced by LLMs (see Table 5 for detailed results).

kp.k: Exposure differs from earlier automation patterns
kp.d: The authors find positive associations with earlier software, machine-learning suitability and routine-cognitive exposure measures, but negative conditional associations with robotics, manual routineness and the Frey–Osborne automation measure for their primary ratings. They attribute this distinction to limited exposure of physical work. At industry level, information-processing work is highly exposed, while manufacturing, agriculture and mining are less exposed. Productivity growth since 2012 appears unrelated to estimated LLM exposure; the authors treat this as grounds for a possible optimistic scenario, not proof of future productivity gains.
qs: This negative correlation reflects the limited exposure of physical tasks to LLMs.
We analyze exposure by industry and discover that information processing industries (4-digit NAICS) exhibit high exposure, while manufacturing, agriculture, and mining demonstrate lower exposure.
Productivity growth since 2012 and exposure to LLM technologies appear unrelated.

kp.k: General-purpose technology status rests on complementary innovation
kp.d: The authors argue that LLMs exhibit the three characteristics of general-purpose technologies: improving capabilities, economic pervasiveness and complementary innovation. Prior literature supports the improvement criterion, while their task classifications support potential breadth and scope for complementary software. They do not systematically measure adoption. They further predict that economic effects could continue expanding through integration even without additional advances in underlying model capabilities.
qs: This classification requires LLMs to meet three core criteria: improvement over time, pervasiveness throughout the economy, and the ability to spawn complementary innovations (Lipsey et al., 2005).
While LLMs have consistently improved in capabilities over time, their growing economic effect is expected to persist and increase even if we halt the development of new capabilities today.

While our findings suggest that out-of-the-box these models are relevant to a meaningful share of workers and tasks, they also suggest that the software innovations they spawn could drive a much broader impact.

kp.k: Augmentation preceding automation remains a speculative pathway
kp.d: The discussion offers augmentation followed by automation as one possible trajectory, including a scenario in which writers become freelancers before full automation. The paper does not demonstrate this sequence or establish its occurrence in law. The authors call for preparedness for possible economic disruption, refer to existing work on education, training and safety-net reform, and leave specific policy prescriptions outside their scope.
qs: Another is that the initial focus will be on augmentation, followed by automation (Huang and Rust, 2018).
One way this might take shape is through an augmentation phase where jobs first become more precarious (e.g., writers becoming freelancers) before transitioning to full automation.

Our results examining worker exposure in the United States underscore the need for societal and policy preparedness to the potential economic disruption posed by LLMs and the complementary technologies that they spawn.

kp.k: Subjective labels and task decomposition limit conclusions
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that annotators lack occupational diversity, GPT-4 classifications depend on prompt wording, and no annotation source constitutes definitive ground truth. Task descriptions may omit tacit skills and dependencies; theoretical exposure can differ from practical performance in complex, domain-specific work. The US focus also limits international generalization. These qualifications make the study a forward-looking exposure framework rather than a direct measurement of achieved productivity, legal-service quality or employment effects.
qs: However, this group is not occupationally diverse, potentially leading to biased judgments regarding LLMs’ reliability and effectiveness in performing tasks within unfamiliar occupations.
As a result, we use multiple annotation sources, but none should be considered the definitive ground truth relative to the others.
If indeed, the task-based breakdown is not a valid representation of how most work in an occupation is performed, our exposure analysis would largely be invalidated.
Furthermore, we acknowledge that there may be discrepancies between theoretical and practical performance, particularly in complex, open-ended, and domain-specific tasks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock estimate widespread potential task-level time savings from LLMs, amplified by complementary software; they do not equate exposure with job displacement.
pts.d: This cross-domain study estimates that around 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks exposed, and approximately 19% could have at least half exposed under its preferred beta measure. Direct LLM access potentially accelerates about 15% of tasks; including complementary software raises the task-level share to 47–56%. Exposure means potential completion in at least half the time at equivalent quality, not demonstrated automation or employment loss. The authors argue that LLMs exhibit general-purpose technology characteristics and that complementary innovations could expand their economic effects even without further model advances. Specifically for law, they describe Casetext as enabling quicker, more accurate research through embeddings and summarization, and envisage software aggregating cases and drafting tailored research memoranda. They also present augmentation followed by automation as one possible trajectory, not a finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence consists of human and GPT-4 classifications of occupational tasks, rather than measured workplace productivity or job losses.
pts.d: The supplied text is the August 2023 v5 working paper, identified in the document header alongside its June 2024 Science publication. The study uses O*NET 27.2, encompassing 1,016 occupations, 19,265 tasks and 2,087 detailed work activities, linked to BLS employment and wage data from 2020 and 2021. Authors and annotators experienced in reviewing OpenAI model outputs supplied human labels; an early GPT-4 classified task–occupation pairs using a prompt adjusted for agreement with author labels. Alpha counts directly exposed tasks, beta counts direct exposure plus half of software-dependent exposure, and zeta counts both fully. The 47–56% range reflects human and model task-level estimates, not a confidence interval. Comparisons with earlier exposure measures and skill regressions support the authors' distributional analysis. They acknowledge subjective labeling, insufficient occupational diversity, prompt sensitivity, and uncertainty about task decomposition. Casetext is an illustrative product example, without a reported legal-research experiment or quantified accuracy comparison.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No adoption or development timetable is predicted; potential gains depend on equivalent quality, complementary innovation, organizational adaptation and trustworthy outputs.
pts.d: The analysis assesses capabilities and anticipated tooling from the working paper's 2023 vantage point, not realized effects by the 2024 publication date. Its exposure threshold is a potential time reduction of at least 50% while retaining equivalent quality. Direct exposure excludes vision capabilities, which enter the software-expanded category. Software-dependent estimates presume additional tools can be developed and integrated. The authors explicitly distinguish technical feasibility from actual productivity and automation outcomes, noting investment, regulation, preferences, incentives, data availability, safety and organizational redesign as adoption conditions. In law, verification of original documents and independent research are specifically identified as constraints on usefulness. The authors do not establish that these checks can safely be eliminated. They acknowledge that practical time savings may be below their estimates and that theoretical performance can diverge from performance on complex, domain-specific work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Potential exposure spans US occupations, with higher-wage, writing-intensive and programming-intensive work generally more exposed; legal support roles appear among highly exposed occupations.
pts.d: The authors find higher wages generally associated with greater exposure, writing and programming skill importance positively associated with exposure, and science and critical thinking negatively associated. Exposure rises through Job Zone 4 and remains similar or declines in Job Zone 5. Lawyers are examples of Job Zone 5 occupations, but that zone's averages are not lawyer-specific estimates. Table 4 assigns Legal Secretaries and Administrative Assistants 100% exposure under the model's upper-bound zeta measure; Court Reporters and Simultaneous Captioners receive 92.9% direct exposure and 96.4% beta exposure from the model. These are shares of equally weighted tasks potentially accelerated, not percentages of workers displaced or work fully automated. Lawyers and firms are also potential users of specialized research tools. The study does not separately estimate effects by law-firm size, client segment or access-to-justice population. It emphasizes US workers and cautions against generalizing internationally; the underlying government data primarily cover documented, non-self-employed workers in the formal economy.
